input.question: Is there any data available on self reported life satisfaction in the USSR? How did its break-up affect life satisfaction?
input.ground_truth: I don't know much about the outright reporting of life satisfaction in the USSR, but if you look at statistics of before and after the fall of the Soviet Union in terms of things such as life expectancy, infant mortality, alcoholism, drug abuse, homicide, suicide, and domestic violence, and compare that to the opinion polls of Russian citizens today asking how many of them wish for a return of the Soviet Union, I feel this could give an impression. As an example of what I'm talking about, in 1985 the average life expectancy for a Russian was around 67 years old; by the mid-1990s, for Russian men, life expectancy was well below 60. Rates of births per woman fell from 1.9 to 1.4 from 1990 to 1994, and rates of alcoholism, suicide, and homicide doubled.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Is there any data available on self reported life satisfaction in the USSR? How did its break-up affect life satisfaction?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a big box of toys, and you ask all your friends how happy they are with their toys. In the USSR, which was like a big country that no longer exists, people didn’t always get to say what they really thought about their toys (or how happy they were with life). Sometimes, the grown-ups in charge would tell them what to say.

But some brave people did ask questions and wrote down what others said, even if it wasn’t always easy. So we have a few pieces of paper (that’s what “data” means) that show some people felt okay, but many felt like they didn’t have enough good toys or couldn’t choose what they wanted.

When the big country broke into smaller countries (that’s what happened when the USSR ended), some people got more choices and more things they liked. But for some people, things got harder at first—like not having enough food or feeling scared. So, some people felt happier, but others felt sadder or more worried. It’s a bit like when you share your toys with friends: some friends are happy, but sometimes someone misses having all their toys to themselves.

So, we have a little bit of information, but not a lot, because it was hard to ask questions in the old country. And after the country broke apart, some people were happier, and some were not.
